name: Rifaximin
sections: Red-orange crystalline powder, practically insoluble in water.

Approved in the USA for travellers' diarrhoea (2004), hepatic encephalopathy recurrence (2010) and IBS-D (2015). First approval/introduction: Italy 1987 (Alfa Wassermann); US FDA 2004 (Salix Pharmaceuticals).

Binds bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase beta-subunit, inhibiting RNA synthesis. Minimal absorption gives high intraluminal concentrations active against Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic enteric bacteria; reduces ammonia-producing gut flora. Receptor / target profile: Binds the beta-subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, inhibiting transcription.
Hepatic (CYP3A4) for the small absorbed fraction
Summary: <0.4% systemically absorbed; excreted almost entirely unchanged in faeces.
Reduction in risk of recurrence of overt hepatic encephalopathy (550 mg)
Travellers' diarrhoea caused by non-invasive E. coli
Hepatic encephalopathy: 550 mg twice daily (with lactulose)
IBS-D: 550 mg three times daily for 14 days (may be repeated up to twice for recurrence)
Travellers' diarrhoea: 200 mg three times daily for 3 days
SIBO: 400 mg three times daily or 550 mg three times daily for 14 days
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Use with caution in Child-Pugh C (higher exposure).
Not effective for diarrhoea with fever or blood in stool (invasive pathogens)
Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) – increased exposure
May cause reddish discolouration of urine
Peripheral oedema, nausea, dizziness (in hepatic encephalopathy)
Clinical response; C. difficile if diarrhoea worsens.
Bass et al., NEJM 2010 – rifaximin reduced breakthrough hepatic encephalopathy and hospitalisations.
TARGET 1 & 2 (Pimentel et al., NEJM 2011) – relief of global IBS-D symptoms and bloating.
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
